newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - Dlr/mark vols up as mark nears year low.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Dlr/mark vols up as mark nears year low.

text.p: Implied volatilities for short-dated dollar/mark options were firmer in mid-morning trade on Monday, although off the day's highs, as the U.S. dollar came close to setting a 22-month high.
The dollar continued to flirt with 1.5470 marks which put the May 28 year-high of 1.5488 in sight. If that level is broken, the mark will be trading at levels not seen since January 1995.
"It hasn't been dramatic, like a big fall, but it has certainly been relentless," said one OTC options dealer of the dollar's rally and subsequent rise in implied volatility.
"You've got to see 1.54 (marks per dollar) as being pretty significant," he said.

Players who have taken on short positions in recent weeks, on the assumption the dollar was topping out, have become increasingly nervous, he said. Their attempts to cover positions are helping to drive up volatility.
At 1040 CST/1640 GMT, implied volatility for one-month dollar/mark options was 6.7/6.9 percent, up sharply from Friday but down from the U.S. opening level of 7.05 percent, dealers said.
The one-month 25 delta dollar/mark risk reversal, which compares premium for puts and calls, had flipped to show at .05/.35 percent bias for mark puts.
Another OTC dealer said the mark/French cross rate was also affecting dollar/mark volatility.
With the unexpected testing of a cross rate of 3.40 francs per mark late last week, implied volatilities spiked up to 2.8/3.2 percent across the curve, the dealer said.
Prior to that, one-month mark/French had been trading at 1.8/2.2 percent, he said.
"The market's always a little bit fearful of a French devaluation," the dealer said.

The mark was trading off its lows against the franc on Monday following a weekend meeting between French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl. Chirac reaffirmed support for a stable franc/mark exchange rate at that meeting.
In contrast to dollar/mark, implied volatility for one-month dollar/yen, which last week had traded at levels identical to those of dollar/mark, was flat at 6.1/6.4 percent.
"It's basically dead in the water as we hover around that 113.75 level," the first dealer said.

The yen rose overnight after Japan's central bank governor Yasuo Matsushita said the Japanese recovery appeared to be gaining strength, although he added that interest rates would be kept low to maintain momentum. By mid-morning in the U.S. session, dollar/yen appeared to have stabilized, as had implied volatility.
